meta.title: Reinforcement learning for co-planar multi-target mission planning with a solar sail in Low Earth Orbit
meta.authorsHtml: Arturo De Marinis<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Fernando Gámez Losada<sup>1</sup>, Jeannette Heiligers<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Active Debris Removal (ADR) is a critical priority to ensure the continuity and security of space activities in low Earth orbit. We investigate, in this paper, the design of solar sail missions preparatory for ADR, with the objective of visiting co-planar circular orbits in the order that minimizes the mission transfer time. This challenge is a one-dimensional traveling salesperson problem, which we solve by using Reinforcement Learning (RL). The employment of RL is feasible thanks to the patched method, a semi-analytical technique to estimate the transfer time of trajectories, without numerically integrating and optimizing them. This is decisive for training RL models. We target approximately dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbits between 700 km and 900 km, where there is high density of debris objects, and constant exposure to sunlight during the year provides ideal conditions for solar sail propulsion. The RL approach is validated against Exhaustive Search (when feasible) and Ant Colony Optimization, and against two simple baselines, i.e. Ascending Sorting and Descending Sorting. The results of the numerical experiments demonstrate that RL effectively identifies optimal and near-optimal transfer sequences, matching the performance of traditional metaheuristics, and offering a framework for rapid mission planning in orbital environment.

blocks.html: Active Debris Removal (ADR) is a topic of great importance nowadays due to the dense collection of space debris pieces orbiting the Earth, that constantly puts in danger active satellites and compromises space missions. It is estimated that over 50,000 debris objects with a diameter larger than 10 cm populate the space environment, see [1], with approximately 40,000 ones tracked by space surveillance systems, see [2]. Most pieces of debris, in particular, occupy the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) environment. There, the debris population is so dense that, even with a complete halt of launches, it would keep growing due to collisions, see [3], leading to the occurrence of the Kessler Syndrome [4, 5]. The Kessler Syndrome is a catastrophic scenario of chain reaction of debris collisions, that would make the space environment extremely hazardous and could even compromise the operability of certain orbital regions. Consequently, the development of effective removal technologies for LEO debris objects is a critical priority, see [6, 7].

ADR missions performed so far and planned for the future are based on chemical propulsion and for the removal of one target, see [8–10]. Despite ion (electric) propulsion has been frequently proposed in academic papers for future multi-target missions, due to its high fuel efficiency [11–13], the technology implemented in recent years has relied on chemical thrusters for their higher thrust and technological maturity.

In this paper, we focus on solar sail propulsion [14] – a technology suitable for multi-target missions due to its potentially endless propulsion capability – for ADR missions in LEO. However, our understanding of what is achievable with solar sail technology around planetary bodies is very limited, since most solar sail astrodynamics research is focused on heliocentric trajectories [14–16]. Some solar sail missions have flown around Earth [17–20], with ACS3 [21] being the most recent example, but with no complete theoretical understanding of the dynamics, possibly due to the great challenges posed by planet-bounded sailing [14]. Previous research on planet-centered solar sailing focuses on escape trajectories or open-ended trajectories [22–28], and the few works that consider orbital transfers do not tackle the problem in a generalized fashion [29–32]. Among these mentioned works, Kelly et al. in [30] and Bianchi et al. in [32] propose solar sail missions for ADR from Geostationary Orbit (GEO) and LEO respectively. However, they focus only on the removal of one debris object, and they leave multi-target ADR missions as an open problem.

A fundamental contribution to the understanding of planet-bounded sailing is due to Gámez Losada et al. in [33, 34]. Here, the authors study the transfer problem of a solar sail between two co-planar circular orbits, providing a semi-analytical technique, the patched method, to compute the transfer time from the change in orbital radius.
Motivated by the above-mentioned study, we design two solar sail missions preparatory for an ADR multi-target mission in LEO:
1. given a set of co-planar circular orbits, a solar sail has
to visit all orbits once in the order that minimizes the overall transfer time;

2. given a set of co-planar circular orbits, a solar sail has to visit all orbits once, and then go back to the starting one, in the order that minimizes the overall transfer time. Since the circular orbits lie in the same orbital plane, each orbit is uniquely identified by its altitude or radius. Therefore, these missions are one-dimensional traveling salesperson problems (1D-TSP), combinatorial optimization problems that we approach with Reinforcement Learning (RL), in particular with the Attention Model and with the Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima, see [35–37]. Here, the patched method is essential for training the RL model, without the computational overload of computing hundreds of thousands of trajectories to get their transfer time.

We validate the results obtained by using RL with Exhaustive Search (ES) when the number of orbits is small, and we consider Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) [38] as validation method when the number of orbits is large, and ES thus becomes unfeasible. We choose ACO as validation method because it is used by the winners [39–41] of the 9th edition of the Global Trajectory Optimization Competition (GTOC) [42] to solve the TSP arising in the GTOC assignment. Since then, it has been used as validation method for most of the new techniques tackling the TSP, see [43–47]. As further simple baselines, we also consider Ascending Sorting and Descending Sorting.
The design of a complete ADR mission in LEO with solar sail technology is left as next step of this study.
This paper is organized as follows.

In Section 2, we introduce the preliminaries needed for the development of the paper. In particular, in Section 2.1, we define the reference frames where we formulate our mission scenarios, and in Section 2.2, we recall the patched method from [33, 34].

In Section 3, we report the results of our numerical experiments. Specifically, we first declare the optimal orbital regime to visit with a solar sail. Then, we present the numerical results for the two mission scenarios that we are designing.
In Section 4, we outline our conclusions and future perspectives.
As in [33], we introduce two inertial reference frames centered at the Earth: the ecliptic reference frame E(xe, ye, ze) and the orbital reference frame I(x, y, z).

The ecliptic reference frame has xe-axis aligned with the Sun-Earth direction, ˆS, at the initial epoch, i.e. the autumnal equinox. The ze-axis matches the ecliptic north pole and the ye-axis completes the right-handed triad. The orientation of the orbital plane is provided by the inclination, i, and the right ascension of the ascending node (RAAN), Ω, in the ecliptic frame. The inclination i is measured from the ze-axis, while the RAAN Ωis measured from the xeaxis. The Sun-Earth direction ˆS rotates counter-clockwise in the ecliptic plane with a period, P, equal to a solar year. Figure 1 shows the ecliptic plane and the orientation of the orbital plane.

blocks.caption: Ecliptic reference frame E(xe, ye, ze) and orientation of the orbital plane, taken from [33].
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The orbital reference frame has x-axis coinciding with the line of nodes, the z-axis is parallel to the orbit’s angular momentum vector, h, and the y-axis completes the right-handed triad. The orbital reference frame is used to formulate the Equations of Motion, see [33, Section II].

We define the aspect angle β as the angle between the Sun-Earth direction ˆS and the orbit’s angular momentum vector h. The aspect angle determines the illumination status of the orbital plane: for β = 0◦and β = 90◦, the orbital plane is perpendicular and parallel to the incoming sunlight, respectively. The aspect angle changes periodically due to the yearly motion of ˆS. We assume the Sun to be infinitely far away from Earth so that all Sun rays are parallel to ˆS.
We consider the transfer by a solar sail from one circular orbit to another circular orbit, both lying in the same orbital plane, and we are interested in computing the transfer time.

Gámez Losada et al. in [33] tackle this problem by proposing the co-planar patched multi-revolution circularto-circular (PMC2C) transfer. The PMC2C transfer is a continuous sequence of single-revolution circular-to-circular (SC2C) transfers (see [34] by Gámez Losada et al.). Here, each SC2C transfer is computed by maximizing the change in orbital radius in one orbital revolution, defined to be the performance of the SC2C transfer. Then, the transfer time of the PMC2C transfer is obtained by accumulating the transfer times of each SC2C transfer. Since a PMC2C transfer is the aggregation of SC2C transfers, the PMC2C transfer is not globally optimal. Nevertheless, it is a valid solar sail transfer trajectory between two arbitrary circular co-planar orbits, and the PMC2C transfer time is an approximation of the optimal transfer time.

Gámez Losada et al. in [33] further propose a semianalytical technique to compute the transfer time ∆ν (in years) corresponding to a PMC2C transfer with a normalized radius (altitude) change ∆ρ, without computing numerically the PMC2C transfer itself. This technique is called patched method, and the formula at its foundation is

blocks.alt: Z 1+∆ρ ρ1+s = ηρ0 Z ν0+∆ν χdν, dρ P T0 ν0 1

blocks.html: where s > 0 is a coefficient that quantifies how performance varies with orbital radius, ηρ0 and T0 are respectively the reference performance and the orbital period of the solar sail at the initial condition of the PMC2C transfer, P is the orbital period of Earth, ν0 is the initial time of the transfer, and χ is a real function of the aspect angle β. Remark 2.1 The accuracy and bias of the patched method relative to the numerical integration, and its approximation error, are quantified in [33, 34].

We report in this section the results of the numerical experiments that we have carried out. We start by declaring the orbital regime that we consider, optimal to visit with a solar sail. Then, we present the numerical results for the proposed mission scenarios.

Here, we discuss the orbital regime that is optimal to visit with a solar sail. Indeed, a solar sail needs constant exposure to sunlight to have maximum thrusting capabilities, see [34], and this requirement makes some orbits more favorable to visit than others. The orbits that are constantly exposed to sunlight throughout the year are those lying in orbital planes approximately perpendicular to the incoming sunlight, that is with aspect angle β between 0 and 35 degrees. Orbits that approximately satisfy this requirement are dawn-dusk Sun-Synchronous Orbits (SSOs) [48]. Since our future goal is to remove pieces of debris, we look at the debris catalog from Space-Track.org, and we extract the altitude distribution of debris objects in dawn-dusk SSO, plotted in Figure 2, and the eccentricity of their orbits. We notice that most of the extracted debris objects have an altitude between 700 km and 900 km, and their orbits are approximately circular.

blocks.caption: Altitude distribution of dawn-dusk SSO debris.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: This analysis suggests us to consider dawn-dusk SSOs with altitude between 700 km and 900 km. We notice, however, that SSOs with different altitudes have different inclinations, so they are not co-planar orbits. Nevertheless, for the altitude range [700 km, 900 km], the corresponding SSO inclination range in the Earth Centered Inertial frame is approximately [98◦, 99◦], and a solar sail can successfully execute maneuvers to slightly change its inclination [49]. Therefore, it is a valid approximation to consider “coplanar SSOs” in the altitude range [700 km, 900 km] with an inclination of 98.5◦and with a RAAN Ω= 90◦at the initial time, set to be the autumnal equinox. Such range of orbits is approximately perpendicular to the incoming sunlight during the whole year, and is thus optimal for solar sail missions.

We consider two sets of circular “co-planar SSOs”, see Tables 1 and 2, in the altitude range [700 km, 900 km], lying in an orbital plane with constant inclination 98.5◦and with a RAAN Ω= 90◦at the initial time, set to be the autumnal equinox.
We aim to solve the following mission scenarios for the given sets of orbits.
1. Mission scenario 1: a solar sail has to visit all orbits in Tables 1 and 2 once in the order that minimizes the
overall transfer time.

2. Mission scenario 2: a solar sail has to visit all orbits in Tables 1 and 2 once, and then go back to the starting one, in the order that minimizes the overall transfer time. These scenarios are 1D-TSP, that we solve by using the Attention Model (AM) based on REINFORCE, with a deterministic greedy rollout as baseline, proposed by Kool et al. in [36], and the Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) based on a modified REINFORCE algorithm that forces diverse rollouts towards all optimal solutions, proposed by Kwon et al in [37]. Both the AM and the POMO take in input the list of orbits to visit, and return as output an ordered list of orbits that (sub-optimally) minimizes the transfer time. The reward function that we aim to maximize is minus the transfer time, that we compute by using the patched method, see Section 2.2. We compare the results by RL with Exhaustive Search (ES) – only for the orbits in Table 1 –, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), Ascending Sorting (AS) and Descending Sorting (DS).
Mission scenario 1. The results for mission scenario 1 for the orbits in Tables 1 and 2 are collected in Tables 3 and 4, respectively. The transfer time is measured in years.

blocks.html: We notice that both RL models, the AM and the POMO, do not return the optimal solution, computed with ES and ACO for the set of five orbits, and with ACO for the set of ten orbits. However, the deviation in the reward is in the fifth decimal digit for the solution by the AM, and in the third decimal digit for the solution by the POMO, so we can still be satisfied with the results by RL. Furthermore, the solution by AM corresponds to the one by DS, while the solution by the POMO corresponds to the one by AS. Remark 3.1 In both mission scenarios, the advantage of using RL over ES and ACO is that RL returns a solution instantaneously. It could take a long time to train an RL model but, once it has been trained, the model returns a solution instantly.

In Table 7, we report the runtime of ES and ACO for the five orbits in Table 1, and the runtime of ACO for the ten orbits in Table 2, for mission scenarios 1 and 2. In particular, for the ten orbits in Table 2, we appreciate the instantaneous runtime of RL over the long runtime of ACO.

In the context of planning multiple missions, obtaining a solution instantly, even if suboptimal, is more valuable than obtaining the optimal solution at great computational cost. Remark 3.2 RL models depend heavily on random numbers, such as initial network weights, data shuffling, and stochastic action choices during REINFORCE training. A single training run could achieve great results purely by chance.

blocks.html: To show that the employed RL models reliably converge to good solutions every time we train them, rather than just on one lucky trial, we need to train and evaluate the RL models across multiple random seeds.

We perform such statistical validation for the AM to solve mission scenarios 1 and 2 for the five orbits in Table 1. We consider five seeds, namely 52, 123, 777, 2026, and 9999. The solutions returned by the AM, trained across all considered seeds, match the ones by the AM in Tables 3 and 5. Therefore, the performed statistical validation certifies the reliability of the RL approach. Remark 3.3 To demonstrate true combinatorial intelligence of the RL models, we solve mission scenarios 1 and 2 for a significantly large number of orbits, namely 25 equidistant circular orbits from the altitude of 710 km to the altitude of 890 km, lying in an orbital plane with constant inclination 98.5◦and with a RAAN Ω= 90◦at the initial time, set to be the autumnal equinox.

The solutions by the AM and the POMO, for both mission scenarios, show the same ordering of the 25 orbits as the solutions by the AM and the POMO in Tables 3 to 6 for the orbits in Tables 1 and 2. This shows true combinatorial intelligence of the employed RL models.

It would be also possible to consider more than 25 orbits to certify the combinatorial intelligence of the employed RL models. We expect, also in this case, that the ordered sequence of orbits given by the AM and the POMO, for both mission scenarios, show the same ordering of the orbits as in the solutions by the AM and the POMO in Tables 3 to 6 for the orbits in Tables 1 and 2.

The numerical experiments have been performed by using MATLAB R2025a and Python, in particular the PyTorch library RL4CO [50], on a laptop with a RAM of 16 GB and processor Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 155U (1.70 GHz). The AM and the POMO, with an embedding dimension set to be 128, are trained with a batch size of 256, a training data size of 15000 and a validation data size of 1500, for 5 and 10 epochs when 5 and 10 (and 25) orbits are considered, respectively. The values of the physical constants used in the numerical experiments, mentioned in Section 2, are taken from [33].

The results presented in this paper show the effectiveness of Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve the combinatorial optimization problem of co-planar multi-target solar sail mission planning. By tackling the one-dimensional traveling salesperson problem of orbital transfers with the Attention Model (AM) and the Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO), we have demonstrated that RL models reliably identify optimal and near-optimal orbital sequences that minimize the transfer time.

A key factor of this success has been the use of the patched method to compute transfer times. It provides the rapid estimation of transfer times necessary for training RL models, without the high computational overload of numerical integration of trajectories. Furthermore, focusing on debris objects in dawn-dusk Sun-Synchronous orbits ensures that a solar sail maintains the aspect angle required for near-constant sunlight exposure and, thus, optimal propulsion.

Our numerical experiments show that, for mission scenario 1, the RL identifies the optimal solution found by Descending Sorting (DS), Exhaustive Search (ES) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO). In the more complex mission scenario 2, while the RL models deviate from the optimal solution found by ES and ACO, the variation in the reward occurs only at the fifth and third decimal digit for the AM and the POMO respectively, which is negligible.

The presented research provides a robust AI-driven foundation for the rapid design of missions preparatory for Active Debris Removal, powered by solar sail technology. Future research will move beyond co-planar orbital transfers to include non co-planar ones, and the rendezvous problem of high-priority targets from debris catalogs.
